title: A Practical Guide to Visual Assessment and Rehabilitation After Stroke for Physiotherapists New to Stroke Care
content: Visual impairment affects approximately three out of four people admitted to hospital with acute stroke; however, more than half of those with a new impairment do not report visual symptoms. Because vision guides balance, transfers, walking and navigation, an unrecognized visual deficit can be mistaken for weakness, inattention or poor motivation. This narrative review, written for physiotherapists new to stroke care, synthesizes guideline, cohort, diagnostic accuracy, trial and systematic review evidence. It describes five overlapping categories of visual impairment after stroke: reduced central vision, visual field loss, eye movement disorders, visual neglect and higher level perceptual disorders. It then proposes a seven step bedside screen that requires simple equipment and concludes with observation of the patient during mobility. For each category, practical treatment strategies are paired with a summary of the evidence, which remains limited for widely used interventions such as scanning training and prism adaptation. Referral pathways and visual red flags requiring urgent medical review are also outlined. Physiotherapists are well placed to detect visual impairment early, describe its effect on movement and safety, adapt therapy and refer promptly, and structured visual screening should form part of every stroke physiotherapy assessment.
